questions.prompt: In a weight-stationary systolic array, what moves and what stays?
options: Weights stay in the cells; activations move right and partial sums move down
Everything stays; a crossbar routes values
Outputs stay; weights and activations move
questions.explanation: Each cell keeps one weight while data flows past it.

questions.prompt: Why does a systolic array need so little memory bandwidth per operation?
options: Each value read is reused by every cell it passes through, and cells only talk to neighbours
questions.explanation: Reuse is built into the dataflow.

questions.prompt: According to the paper's rooflines, what limited most of Google's production inference workloads on the TPU?
questions.explanation: The MLPs and LSTMs sat left of the ridge point.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't the workloads simply use a bigger batch to raise intensity?
options: The 99th-percentile latency deadline caps the batch size
The Weight FIFO is too small
questions.explanation: Inference serving trades throughput for latency.

questions.prompt: A 128×128 array of 8-bit MACs runs at 1 GHz with 100 GB/s of weight bandwidth. Ridge point in MACs per weight byte?
Which of these followed this paper?
options: TPU v2 with HBM and bfloat16, for training
Accelerators designed around keeping matrix units fed
questions.explanation: Matrix units became the centre of AI hardware.
